# Digest G — Phil 4:1–23

**Source:** G. Walter Hansen, *The Letter to the Philippians* (PNTC)  
**Slice:** `slice_G_4_1-23.txt` (raw lines 2489–2777)  
**Section coverage:** VII. Final Appeals (4:1–9); VIII. Thanks for Gifts from Partners (4:10–20); IX. Greetings and Grace (4:21–23)  
**Extractor note:** Digest only — no wiki edits. All claims attributed to Hansen.

---

## Key structural points (Hansen)

1. **4:1–3** — Affectionate address + “therefore” grounded in 3:7–21 (righteousness by faith; enemies of the cross; heavenly citizenship; Christ’s return) → stand firm; Euodia and Syntyche named as focus of church disunity; true companion enlisted to help reconcile them; co-workers; book of life.
2. **4:4–9** — Imperative series forming “alternative political body” under Christ not Caesar: rejoice; gentleness; Lord near; anxiety → prayer/petition/thanksgiving; peace of God guards; virtue list (Hellenistic/Stoic vocabulary) + practice Paul’s teaching/example → God of peace with you.
3. **4:10–20** — Acknowledgment of gifts via Epaphroditus; “thankless thanks” problem; contentment (autarkeia) redefined vs Stoic self-sufficiency; 4:13 limited by context (need/plenty); partnership giving/receiving unique to Philippians; fragrant offering; God will supply; doxology.
4. **4:21–23** — Greet every saint; brothers with Paul; all saints especially Caesar’s household (imperial slaves/freedmen/civil service); grace with your spirit; Amen.

---

## Claims

### VII.A — Be of One Mind (4:1–3)

**C1.** Hansen holds that Paul’s “lavish outpouring of love” and plea for unity are not in tension: “Paul passionately loves a divided community. He warmly embraces the community and urges the two opposing leaders of warring factions to be reconciled.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~8–9; Phil 4:1–3 opening.

**C2.** “Therefore” (4:1) points back to motives in 3:7–21: righteousness from God through faith in Christ; destiny of enemies of the cross; heavenly citizenship; expectation of Christ’s return to restore all things.  
- *Quote:* “Paul’s commands are not arbitrary assertions of his personal authority. He always bases his imperatives on the solid ground of the indicatives of what Christ has done and will do. Grace always precedes, surrounds, empowers, and concludes the life of obedience.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~11.

**C3.** Letter frame of grace: begins “Grace and peace…” and ends “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.” Hansen: strong exhortations “can be understood and implemented only in the context of the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~11.

**C4.** Five terms of endearment for the Philippians: brothers and sisters; beloved; longed for; joy and crown; beloved (repeated).  
- *Locus:* slice ~13.

**C5.** Familial “brothers and sisters” springs from adoption as children of God through the Son (Hansen cites Gal 4:4–7 sense); points to equality and mutuality among siblings — “No longer does Paul have a spiritual hierarchy: Jews above Gentiles; faultless Hebrews above clueless Hellenists (3:5–6).”  
- *Locus:* slice ~13.

**C6.** “Beloved” twice: Paul expresses his own “all-inclusive, unconditional love,” not only God’s love for believers.  
- *Quote:* “Paul repeatedly tells his friends, ‘I love you. I really love you.’”  
- *Locus:* slice ~15.

**C7.** “Longed for” is unique in the NT; rarity “adds intensity to the emotion of ‘homesick tenderness,’ especially to the pain of separation.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~15.

**C8.** “Joy and crown”: joy is “relational and not situational” and “cannot be shaken or diminished by the circumstances of his life.” Combination evokes Olympic-style victory celebration. Hansen notes possible eschatological reading via 1 Thess 2:19 and Phil 2:16; 3:20–21, but leans that Paul has the **present** in mind: they are already his joy and crown via partnership and citizenship.  
- *Locus:* slice ~17.

**C9.** “Stand firm in the Lord in this way” repeats 1:27 and is defined by parallels:

| Theme | 1:27–28 | 3:18–20 / 4:2 |
|---|---|---|
| Citizenship | worthy of the gospel as citizens of heaven | citizenship in heaven (3:20) |
| Opposition | those who oppose you | enemies of the cross (3:18) |
| Unity | one Spirit, striving together | same mind in the Lord (4:2) |

- Hansen’s three definitions of stand firm: (1) as citizens of heaven, loyalty to heavenly government; (2) commitment to the cross amid enemies of the cross; (3) united in one mind/Spirit — “we cannot stand firm divided and alone.” Capsulated “in the Lord.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~19–39.

**C10.** Adverb “in this way” (houtōs): may point backward (example of Paul, 3:17) or forward (imperatives 4:2–9). Hansen prefers it as **link** between Paul’s example and the following exhortations.  
- *Locus:* slice ~41.

**C11. Euodia and Syntyche — naming and conflict.** Paul repeats “I plead” so as to address each separately and **not take sides**.  
- *Quote:* “No doubt the conflict between these two leaders caused a division between members of the community as people were forced to declare their allegiance to one or the other. But Paul avoids favoritism by respectfully pleading with each one individually.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~43.

**C12.** Euodia and Syntyche: common Greek names on first-century inscriptions. Attempts to identify them with other biblical characters/social groups “have failed.” Naming indicates well-known members causing “serious division by their personal animosity.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~45.

**C13.** Hansen rejects the view that their squabble was minor in a unified church: naming them in a public letter is justified only if the conflict “seriously threatened the unity of the church” — a major cause of disunity addressed throughout the letter.  
- *Quote:* “‘The church was polarized around Euodia and Syntyche, who were the focus of disunity.’”  
- *Locus:* slice ~45.

**C14.** “Same mind in the Lord” (4:2) repeats the major challenge of 2:2 (like-minded, same love, one spirit and mind). Same language **connects church disunity with these two women’s conflict**.  
- *Locus:* slice ~45.

**C15.** “Same mind” = think the same thing, same attitude/opinion/goal; orientation of life “in the Lord” informed by union with the Lord; attitude toward each other as Christ on the way to the cross: not claiming rights for advantage; form of a servant; humility (2:5–8). Hansen does **not** claim Paul discloses specific practical changes needed.  
- *Locus:* slice ~47.

**C16. Cause of conflict — Hansen’s assessment of hypotheses.**  
- Theological-difference hypothesis (perfectionist Jewish vs permissive Hellenist): speculation; “fails to provide adequate evidence that Paul addressed false theological positions held by members of the church in Philippi.”  
- Split over support for Paul (one withdrew, one supported): conflicts with thanksgiving for **all** and partnership (1:3–8; 4:10–18).  
- Hansen’s preferred frame: selfish ambition/rivalry (1:15–17; 2:3) vs humility (2:3, 8; 3:21).  
- *Quote:* “Whatever the specific issues may have been, the conflict was basically caused by pride, selfish ambition, and a spirit of rivalry. These two church leaders were engaged in a power struggle to expand their spheres of influence and control over the church.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~49.

**C17. True companion / yokefellow (4:3).** Paul enlists a third-party go-between/moderator — conflict too deep for the women alone. Emphatic “yes” + “I ask” stresses urgency. Conflict spreading “like a virulent, aggressive form of cancer in the body.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~51.

**C18. Identity of “true companion” — Hansen surveys options; no certainty.**  
Candidates discussed:  
- **Timothy** — adjective “true” (4:3) and cognate “genuine” concern (2:20); son-with-father relation (2:22).  
- **Epaphroditus** — co-worker, fellow soldier, messenger (2:25); almost died (2:30).  
- **Silas** (Acts 16:11–40 travel companion).  
- **Lydia** (first convert/hostess).  
- **Luke** (first “we” section begins at Philippi, Acts 16:11).  
- Proper name **Syzygos** (“yokefellow”).  
- Metaphor for **entire Philippian church** as partner (1:5; 4:15–18).  
- Even **Paul’s wife** considered (yokefellow sometimes = wife).  
- *Quote:* “All of these hypotheses have their advocates, but ‘it is no longer possible to determine with certainty just whom the apostle has in mind.’ No doubt the church knew the true identity of this person…”  
- *Locus:* slice ~53.

**C19.** Verb “help” (συλλαμβάνω sense): strong physical action — “seize, grasp, apprehend, catch, and take hold of together”; arrest of Jesus/Peter; catch of fish; only use by Paul here.  
- *Quote:* “The two women have moved so far apart that the only hope for reconciliation is for Paul’s companion to take hold of them and draw them back together again.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~55.

**C20.** Motivation: “they have contended at my side in the cause of the gospel” — “struggled along with” / “fought” at his side; same verb as 1:27 (striving together). Not spectators; active participants who “struggled and suffered along with Paul to advance the gospel.” Full members of mission team **along with Clement and the rest of my co-workers**.  
- *Locus:* slice ~57.

**C21. Clement.** Background unavailable; Latin name “may indicate his Roman origin”; good reputation — named as example of one who contended with Paul.  
- *Locus:* slice ~57.

**C22. Book of life.** Names of co-workers not listed but written in the book of life; Jewish tradition + Luke 10:20; Heb 12:23; Rev 3:5 etc. Eschatological note with heavenly citizenship (3:20).  
- *Quote:* “The citizens of the Roman colony of Philippi who have their names recorded in a civic register of citizens know that they have a duty to live in harmony and peace with one another. The citizens of the colony of heaven in the Roman colony of Philippi who have their names written in the book of life in heaven are called by their Lord above all powers to live in peace with one another.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~59.

---

### VII.B — Rejoice in the Lord (4:4–9)

**C23.** Final imperatives are not rote ethics or mere Hellenistic handbook; “integrally related to the major themes of the entire letter and the specific conditions of the church in Philippi.”  
- *Quote:* These guidelines lead the church to be “‘an alternative political body, ruled by a different Lord, to that body constituted by citizens of Philippi under the dominion of Caesar.’”  
- *Locus:* slice ~67.

**C24. Rejoice always (4:4).** Theme of joy throughout letter always tied to concrete contexts (1:18; 2:2; 2:17–18; 2:29; 3:1; 4:10). Command in 4:4 still allows connection: unity–joy link (2:2) with Euodia/Syntyche reconciliation; joyful worship unites. Sets tone for following imperatives. Written from prison to suffering Christians: cheerful attitude “dominant theme.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~69–71.

**C25.** “In the Lord” is the key: despite anxiety-producing circumstances, “a defiant ‘Nevertheless!’” — relationship with Lord central. Psalms heritage (Ps 97:1; 100:1); vision of every tongue confessing Jesus is Lord (2:11). Double command rejects objection that rejoicing in suffering is inappropriate.  
- *Quote:* “In no way is Paul simply advocating a positive mental attitude or urging his readers to ‘cheer up’ and ‘have a nice day.’” Double joy from knowing “resurrection power of Christ and participation in his sufferings (3:10) in his Roman prison.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~73–75.

**C26. Gentleness (4:5).** “Not insisting on every right of letter of law or custom, yielding, gentle, kind, courteous, and tolerant.” Aristotle: equitable, does not stand on rights unduly. Evident **to all** (not only friends/Christians) — reputation of courtesy especially under hostility. Parallel Wisdom of Solomon 2:19 (testing the righteous for gentleness under torture). Suffering tests gentleness; defensive responses natural.  
- *Locus:* slice ~77–79.

**C27. “The Lord is near.”** Encouragement for gentleness under suffering; imminent coming of Savior (3:20–21); Mark 13:29; Jas 5:8; Rev 1:3; 22:10; Marana tha (1 Cor 16:22). Even under Caesar as Lord, courteous leniency possible because Christ the Lord is coming to bring all under control (3:21).  
- *Locus:* slice ~81.

**C28. Anxiety and prayer (4:6).** Present prohibition: stop habitual anxiety. Same verb positive of Timothy’s genuine concern (2:20) — Philippians “crossed the line” to over-concern. Causes in letter: welfare of Paul/Epaphroditus (1:12; 2:26); persecution threats (1:29–30). Comprehensive: “nothing, absolutely nothing.” Positive comprehensive: “in everything.”  
- *Quote:* “‘To begin by praising God for the fact that in this situation, as it is, he is so mightily God — such a beginning is the end of anxiety.’”  
- *Locus:* slice ~83–85.

**C29. Three prayer terms + thanksgiving.**  
- **Prayer** — often intercession; overcomes anxious thoughts about others.  
- **Petition** — urgent request for a need, to God only; Paul/Philippians pray for each other in shared struggle (1:4, 19, 30).  
- **Requests** — naming specific items (cf. Luke 23:24; 1 John 5:15). Not “vague generalities and amorphous meditation.”  
- “Let your requests be made known to God” = full self-disclosure / dependence, not that God is ignorant. Preposition “to” = orientation toward God.  
- *Locus:* slice ~85–87.

**C30. Thanksgiving.** Models 1:3–5; confident petitions rest on grateful remembrance (1:6). Lack of thanksgiving → idolatry/futile thinking (Rom 1:21–25); “turns off the power in prayer”; prayer becomes complaining. Link to 2:14 (without grumbling) via 4:6 thanksgiving.  
- *Locus:* slice ~89.

**C31. Peace of God (4:7) as result.** Conjunction “and” introduces result of v. 6 prayer. Condition is not that all requests are granted, but that requests are made known with thanksgiving.  
- *Quote:* “God’s peace is not the result of the power of our prayers or the effectiveness of our prayers. Prayer is not auto-suggestion, a form of self-hypnosis… ‘Peace is always the gift of God rather than humanly devised or achieved.’”  
- *Locus:* slice ~91.

**C32. Peace of God — dual sense.** (1) Peace God himself has — “calm serenity that characterizes God’s very nature”; God of peace (v. 9). (2) Peace God gives — inward soul-peace grounded in God’s presence/promise. Opposite of anxiety; deeper Hebraic **shalom** = well-being, especially social harmony; “emphatically social concept”; peace with God and one another. In Philippians context continues like-mindedness theme (2:2; 4:2): corporate prayer → gift of peace in troubled relationships; same-mind command fulfilled by God’s peace when church prays.  
- *Locus:* slice ~93–95.

**C33. “Transcends all understanding” — two interpretations; Hansen’s preference.**  
1. Human reason cannot comprehend God’s peace (Calvin; Silva) — unexpected in prison/quarrel.  
2. God’s peace **superior** to human reason/planning for resolving conflict and anxiety.  
Hansen: second “seems to fit best” with the promise that peace will **guard** hearts and minds.  
- *Locus:* slice ~97–99, 101.

**C34. Guard image and pax Romana.** Guard image from Roman garrison at Philippi keeping *pax Romana*. Verb: provide security/guard/protect; military overtones (cf. 2 Cor 11:32 Damascus).  
- *Quote:* Garrison of Roman peace “could only exert external pressure, but God’s peace guards the interior lives, the hearts and minds, of believers in Christ.” Effectiveness of God’s peacekeeping “far surpassed even the best military minds of the Roman army.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~101.

**C35. Hearts and minds.** Heart = center of inner life (thinking, feeling, volition). Mind/thought = product of intellectual process; here neutral (vs negative uses in 2 Cor). Even Christian hearts susceptible to envy/rivalry (1:15; 2:3–4). Holistic interior of community; **not** reducible to individualistic “peace in my own heart” — misses relational peace (2:1–4; 4:2–3). Guarded **in Christ Jesus** (phrase 8× in letter).  
- *Locus:* slice ~103.

**C36. Virtue list (4:8) structure.** Six adjectives with repeated “whatever” + asyndeton → expansive; two nouns (excellent/praiseworthy) in conditional clauses; climax: “think about these things.” Result of peace-guarded minds focusing on excellence.  
- *Locus:* slice ~105–107.

**C37. Hellenistic/Stoic virtue vocabulary.** Resembles Greek virtue lists; *aretē* (“excellence/virtue”) not elsewhere in Paul — Stoic favorite; Plato’s four cardinals; Aristotle’s moral means; Stoic popular moral teaching; Dio Chrysostom; Plutarch on recollecting good men. Terms *lovely*, *admirable* unique in NT; *noble* mainly Pastorals; *true/right/pure* used in Hellenistic ethical senses differing from Paul’s usual theological usage.  
- *Quote:* Paul “has taken over terms that were current coin in popular moral philosophy, especially in Stoicism.” Desire that church “appreciate all that is good in the surrounding culture” despite opposition (1:28) — not total repudiation. But 4:9 “qualifies and elevates” virtues by redefining via Paul’s teaching and example: “life in Christ brings to fulfillment the highest moral aspirations in the surrounding culture.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~111–113.

**C38. Individual virtues (Hansen’s glosses).**  
- **True:** comprehensive truth; “all truth is God’s truth”; integrate with gospel truth.  
- **Noble:** serious, dignified, honorable; turn from ignoble/vulgar; awe-inspiring/majestic.  
- **Right/just:** here Hellenistic sense of obligatory justice/customs, not primarily dikaios before God; public well-ordered society (cf. Matt 20:4; Col 4:1; Philo).  
- **Pure:** morally blameless; thought-life origin of purity.  
- **Lovely:** pleasure/delight (cf. LXX Esth 5:1b beauty).  
- **Admirable:** praiseworthy/commendable; fair-sounding (*euphēma*).  
- **Excellent / praiseworthy:** assume condition true; *aretē* links to Hellenistic virtue ethics; praiseworthy often of persons — point to people embodying virtues; ultimately fulfilled in Christ and those in Christ, with discerning cultural evaluation.  
- *Think:* careful, pondering, meditative; lifetime of disciplined thought.  
- *Locus:* slice ~115–129.

**C39. 4:9 redefines 4:8; no contrast.** Definite relative “whatever” elaborates “such things” of v. 8. Paul does not correct wrong virtues or juxtapose unrelated topics.  
- Hansen paraphrase: think on selfless love as excellent; message and life devoted to self-emptying love of Christ; put into practice what learned/seen in Paul.  
- *Locus:* slice ~131.

**C40. Four verbs: learned, received, heard, seen.** Learned/received ≈ teaching of gospel; heard/seen ≈ paradigmatic life — distinction not to be pressed because life story parallels gospel narrative. *Receive* as technical term for tradition (1 Cor 15:3; 11:23; etc.) and more than intellectual — contagious power of example; hymn of Christ (2:6–11). Heard/seen echo 1:30 (same struggle); display resurrection power and participation in sufferings (3:10).  
- *Locus:* slice ~133–137.

**C41. “Put into practice.”** Move from contemplation to action; need mentor not only manual for mind of Christ (2:5); repeats 3:17 imitation. Appropriate to Jewish and Greco-Roman teacher–student imitation (Testament of Benjamin; Dio Chrysostom).  
- *Locus:* slice ~139.

**C42. Friendship grounded in virtue, not utility.** Before discussing financial partnership (4:10–18), Paul grounds friendship in virtue (Aristotle perfect friendship of the good; Cicero’s law of honorable friendship; inferior friendships of utility/pleasure easily broken).  
- *Quote:* “By calling the Philippian believers to think about the virtues and to practice his embodiment of the virtues in his Christ-centered teaching and life, Paul places his friendship with them on the firm basis of virtue, above all, virtue in Christ.” Eager that they not misconstrue friendship as merely “giving and receiving” (4:15).  
- *Locus:* slice ~141–143.

**C43. Promise: God of peace will be with you.** Those who think and practice experience God’s presence. God of peace in prayers/promises (1 Thess 5:23; Rom 15:33; 16:20; 2 Cor 13:11). Peace ≈ messianic salvation; objective reconciliation more than subjective tranquility; good order vs disorder (1 Cor 14:33). For church disturbed by prominent leaders’ disunity (4:2), welcome reassurance.  
- Relation of 4:9 to 4:7: presence of God of peace **explains** peace of God guarding hearts; only God’s presence brings his peace; linked to Spirit’s fruit (Gal 5:22).  
- *Locus:* slice ~145–147.

---

### VIII. Thanks for Gifts from Partners (4:10–20)

**C44. Passage problem: “thankless thanks.”** Acknowledges initial and recent gifts (via Epaphroditus) but lacks explicit “thank you”; qualifications of independence (not in need; not desire gifts) make him seem reluctant. Interpreters ask: divided allegiance? Violation of Paul’s no-gift principle? Business partnership contract language? Greco-Roman conventions (verbal gratitude mainly to social superiors; material return expected)?  
- Hansen: explores these; more significantly yields insights into spiritual experience, friendship, and theology of giving.  
- *Quote:* “Paul radically transforms the social convention of partnership in the light of the gospel of Christ.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~158–160.

**C45. Rejoiced greatly in the Lord (4:10).** Adverb “greatly” only here in NT — joy surpasses ordinary. Past tense: likely time of receiving gifts via Epaphroditus (4:18). Focus remains on Lord as Provider → 4:19.  
- *Quote:* “This central focus on God transforms the transaction of giving and receiving among Christians from a human, horizontal exchange to a divine-human, triangular interaction. God initiates giving, empowers givers, supplies gifts, and meets needs.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~162.

**C46. “Renewed your concern” — botanical image.** Plant blooming after dormancy; “at last” = end of inactivity. *Phronein* (concern/mind-set) used 10× in letter — relational attitude (1:7; 2:2, 5; 3:15; 4:2); gifts demonstrate concern; joy because concern displays attitude urged for mutual relations (2:2; 4:2).  
- *Locus:* slice ~164–166.

**C47. Sampley societas thesis vs Peterman.** Sampley: *phronein* evidence of voluntary business partnership (*consensual societas*); partnership lasts while same mind (Gaius). Peterman: same mind does not demand *societas*. Hansen: debate on technical *societas* allowed, but must not miss Paul’s close link of same mind/concern with *koinonia* partnership (4:10 with 4:15–16). Concern = essential expression of partnership.  
- *Locus:* slice ~168.

**C48. Implicit gratitude; no rebuke for dormancy.** Expression of joy not explicit “thank you” but communicates gratitude. Corrective clause: “indeed, you were concerned, but you had no opportunity” — imperfect = continuous concern; financial continuity not condition for friendship continuity. Why no opportunity: mystery — possibly severe trial/poverty (2 Cor 8:1–2) or Paul’s inaccessibility (Caesarea/Rome). Speculation only.  
- *Locus:* slice ~170–172.

**C49. “Not that I am in need” (4:11).** Strong “not that!” (repeated 4:17). Does not deny actual lack of essentials; denies that poverty-relief **caused** his great joy. Refuses role of requester → socially inferior client/patron dependency and reciprocal material obligation.  
- *Quote:* “The triangular nature of the partnership — God, Paul, and the Philippians — changes the expectations of social reciprocity. The partnership is not simply a mutual human exchange of material support; now both sides of the partnership look to God, who will meet all your needs (4:19).”  
- *Locus:* slice ~174–176.

**C50. Contentment / autarkeia — Stoic background and Christian reframing (central).**  
- Learned over lifetime of ups and downs; emphatic “I”; not natural or easy.  
- **Stoic sense:** independent man “sufficient to himself and in need of none else”; resist circumstances by will; Seneca: happy man content with present lot; reason over emotions; emotional detachment. Paul uses popular Stoic vocabulary.  
- **Paul’s redefinition / purpose:** demonstrates friendship not based on need; ancient friendship theory: true friendship between self-sufficient (Aristotle; Cicero) vs inferior utility/pleasure friendships.  
- *Quote (purpose):* “Paul’s statement that he learned to be content is his way of claiming that his friendship with the Philippian believers is true friendship, not a friendship based on utility; he was not looking to his friends with self-interest, depending on them to meet his needs, for he had learned to be content.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~178–186.

**C51. School of contentment (4:12).** Know how “to be humbled” and “to prosper”/abound. Humbled: loss of prestige/status; financial humiliation in gift-context; willingness to accept abasement (passive or active echo of Christ who humbled himself, 2:8). Contentment in prosperity rare (Eccl 5:12; 1 Tim 6:10, 17; Plutarch on endless coveting).  
- *Locus:* slice ~188–188.

**C52. “Learned the secret” (μυέω).** Rare NT hapax-level term; technical for initiation into Hellenistic mystery religions / insider knowledge. Being “inside” = **in Christ**, “in the one who empowers me” (4:13).  
- *Quote:* “Contrary to the cliche that experience is the best teacher, contentment is not learned merely by experience in all the circumstances of life but by being in Christ in any and every situation.” Focus on relationship with Christ, not fluctuating circumstances.  
- *Locus:* slice ~190.

**C53. Plenty and participation in sufferings — apparent tension.** Aspirations of 2:5–8; 3:10 seem to make contentment in plenty hypocritical. Hansen rejects reducing “plenty” only to spiritual abundance (though Paul often uses “abound” spiritually) or equating prison “plenty” with luxury hotels — while noting gifts made him “amply supplied” (4:18). Resolution: rejoiced **in the Lord** not in abundance; sought others’ benefit (4:17); prosperity did not produce self-indulgence, greed, or anxiety-protection of goods.  
- *Locus:* slice ~192.

**C54. Hunger/want vs Stoic apathy.** Contentment ≠ absence of pain. Paul “did not seek to be apathetic or unfeeling, as the Stoics did.” Felt hunger/deprivation; tears (3:18) and great joy (4:10); not anesthetized by reason; passionate self-pouring (2:17). Contentment “flows out of his life in Christ.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~194–196.

**C55. “I can do all this” (4:13) — contextual limit, not prosperity slogan.**  
- TNIV “this” wisely limits “all.”  
- *Quote:* “Paul is not claiming omnipotence, the ability to do all things without exception. Any use of this verse to support a claim or goal of a triumphant, victorious Christian life without weaknesses or limitations conflicts with the immediate context and the wider teaching of Paul.”  
- Contextual “all” = content whatever the circumstances (4:11): poverty/prosperity, well fed/hungry — power to endure extremes “without anxiety, with the peace of God guarding his heart and mind in Christ Jesus (4:6–7).”  
- Strength “in the one who empowers” = incorporative union with Christ (not mere agency “through”); communion with Christ source of strength.  
- Will not let church/gift replace Christ as source; free from depending on own powers or friends’ money. Contentment = active pursuit of knowing/preaching Christ, not passive whatever-will-be.  
- *Locus:* slice ~198–200.

**C56. Yet you did well to share in my troubles (4:14).** Adversative returns to partnership theme after contentment digression. Compound “share with” intensifies mutuality; partnership in gospel advance, Spirit, sufferings of Christ. Philippians participated via Epaphroditus (almost died, 2:30). Troubles = external oppression as prisoner + inward distress. Focus more on relationship than on support amount. Share in troubles (4:14) echoes share in grace (1:7); suffering granted (1:29).  
- *Locus:* slice ~202–204.

**C57. Commendation form vs client “thank you.”** “You did well” = praise for excellent conduct; “more like a teacher congratulating a student” than client thanking patron — avoids social debt of explicit gratitude while rewarding moral value of partnership. Assuages hurt from contentment-without-support claim.  
- *Locus:* slice ~206.

**C58. History of partnership (4:15–16).** “As you Philippians know” = they know and Paul remembers/treasures. Name *Philippenses* = Greek transcription of Latin colonial name (Colonia Iulia Augusta Philippensium) — respect for Roman civic pride.  
- “Early days of acquaintance with the gospel” = Philippians’ beginning with gospel (not Paul’s career start); cf. 1:5 “from the first day”; reminds they received gospel from Paul.  
- Support after departure from Macedonia = support for ministry in **Corinth** (cf. 2 Cor 11:9).  
- *Locus:* slice ~208–214.

**C59. Unique partnership: “not one church… except you only.”** Verb “became a partner”; “giving and receiving” = Hellenistic commercial language (account of debt/credit) **and** nontechnical friendship exchange. Hansen: real financial transactions (past gifts + Epaphroditus delivery) **and** metaphors for spiritual transactions; spiritual foundation in gospel; not reduced to commercial relationship. Exceptional generosity becomes metaphor for God’s generosity in the gospel.  
- *Locus:* slice ~216.

**C60. Thessalonica support (4:16).** Out of chronological sequence: before leaving Macedonia they sent aid “more than once” when Paul was in need in Thessalonica — immediacy and frequency. History of gifts permanently in memory; recent gift not “all that mattered.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~218–220.

**C61. “Not that I desire your gifts” (4:17).** Reinforces 4:11. Possibly counters unfair caricature of clever fundraising, but Hansen finds warm commendation against theory that church divided over supporting him. Primary aim: guard against cultural pressure turning partnership into **patronage** with Paul as subservient client; maintain friendship of equals; reject utilitarian motive.  
- *Locus:* slice ~222.

**C62. Fruit to your account.** Investment language: fruit = advantage/profit increasing to account; daily compounding until day of Christ (links 1:10–11; 2:16; 3:20–21). Fruit = spiritual growth / fruit of righteousness / love abounding (1:9) / Christ-likeness — “Every act of love increased their capacity to love more.” Also God’s material/spiritual provisions (4:19).  
- *Quote:* “Of course, Paul is not teaching a health-and-wealth gospel. He is not assuring his readers that they will experience great material prosperity as a result of their gifts. But he is expressing his genuine desire that they will experience the full spectrum of God’s care just as he has.” Not promise of absence of suffering, but God’s presence/provision in suffering.  
- *Locus:* slice ~224–228.

**C63. Full payment / amply supplied (4:18).** Commercial receipt language: sum paid in full; more than enough; filled to overflowing via Epaphroditus’s delivery. Abundance witness paves way for 4:19 promise (not primarily “please send no more”).  
- *Locus:* slice ~230.

**C64. Fragrant offering, acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God.** Social friendship act = religious worship act.  
- **Fragrant offering** (“odor of fragrance”): Gen 8:21; Exod 29:18; Lev; Christ’s death as pleasing odor (Eph 5:2).  
- **Acceptable sacrifice:** OT offerings; Ps 51:17; Phil 2:17 sacrifice of faith.  
- **Pleasing to God:** Rom 12:1; Heb 13:16.  
- Gifts reframed beyond financial/social value; meaning derived more from givers fulfilling God’s will than from benefit to Paul; threefold cord God–Paul–church.  
- *Locus:* slice ~232–238.

**C65. My God will meet all your needs (4:19).** Friendship reciprocity: Paul in chains cannot return gifts in kind; return comes from “my God.” Possessive “my” = intimacy + expectancy from his own experience of ample supply; “my God… your needs” = God acts on Paul’s behalf for them. Needs primarily material (parallel to Paul’s troubles) **and** spiritual (love, unity, joy, gentleness). Future tense: on time in God’s time — present trouble and final consummation (3:21).  
- *Locus:* slice ~240–248.

**C66. According to riches of his glory in Christ Jesus.**  
1. **According to his riches** — measure of supply matches God’s wealth (2 Cor 6:10; 8:9; Rom 2:4; 11:33; Col/Eph riches texts). Lavish not stingy; **not** get-rich-quick; suffering still characterizes true believers.  
2. **In glory** — transcendence of riches; fully received in glory on day of Christ / body transformation (3:21).  
3. **In Christ Jesus** — address of recipients (echo 1:1); friendship transformed as residents in Christ; enrichment via cross and resurrection; greatest riches = knowing Christ (3:10).  
- *Locus:* slice ~250–256.

**C67. Doxology (4:20).** “My God” (promise) → “our God and Father” (shared worship); glory of Father as in hymn 2:11; not adding to God’s glory but affirming it. Forever and ever = “into the ages of the ages.”  
- **Amen:** strong affirmation; congregational response custom; endorse doxology — “Yes. So shall it be!”  
- *Locus:* slice ~258–262.

---

### IX. Greetings and Grace (4:21–23)

**C68. Greet all God’s people (4:21).** Customary greeting imperative; here leaders greet **each** member for Paul individually (“Paul remembers you”) rather than collective wave; replaces naming individuals.  
- *Quote:* “Perhaps, Paul does not follow his custom of naming individuals because he does not want to give an additional reason for envy and rivalry in an already divided church.”  
- *Locus:* slice ~275–277.

**C69. Saints / God’s people.** “Every saint in Christ Jesus”; bookend with 1:1. Echoes Israel as holy people (Exod 19:4); covenantal position by grace — **position** not moral achievement. Union with Christ basis of sainthood; against defining holiness by ancestry/law-keeping (3:2–6).  
- *Locus:* slice ~277–279.

**C70. Brothers and sisters with me vs all saints (4:21–22).** Smaller circle (like Timothy, Epaphroditus) vs larger “all the saints” in city of imprisonment. Paul builds association of churches; union in Christ transcends social/political divisions.  
- *Locus:* slice ~279–281.

**C71. Caesar’s household (4:22) — Hansen’s identification.**  
- *Quote:* “The household of Caesar consisted of slaves and freed slaves (freedmen) of the emperor. They functioned as managers of the properties and enterprises of the emperor throughout the empire. Some members of Caesar’s household were involved in the administration of the government; they served as civil servants under imperial direction.”  
- If written from Rome, Romans 16 may include names; Aristobulus (16:10) and Narcissus (16:11) connected with Claudius’s household — speculation cannot give certainty for Philippians greetings.  
- **Certainty:** Paul wants Philippians to know imprisonment advanced the gospel (1:12); imperial guard heard; members of Caesar’s household are “saints” greeting Philippi saints.  
- *Quote:* “These simple greetings bear an implicit message to the Philippians: imperial power cannot stop the power of the gospel. Even while Paul in a Roman prison and the believers in Philippi are suffering under imperial authorities, the gospel is claiming the allegiance of imperial agents.” Points toward every knee bowing (2:10–11).  
- *Locus:* slice ~283–287.  
- **Note:** Hansen identifies imperial **slaves/freedmen/civil service**, not merely the emperor’s blood family.

**C72. Grace benediction (4:23).** Repeats opening grace (1:2); sole focus on Lord Jesus Christ implies Christ’s authority to convey grace. Meaning drawn via 2 Cor 8:9 (rich→poor) // Phil 2:6–8, and 2 Cor 12:9 (grace in weakness) // Phil 3:10 resurrection power. Blessing desires experience of cross-shaped self-giving love in relationships **and** resurrection power in suffering worthy of the gospel.  
- *Locus:* slice ~289.

**C73. “With your spirit.”** Distributive singular: “with the spirit of each one of you.” May mean inner self-awareness (1 Cor 2:11) or whole person.  
- *Locus:* slice ~291–293.

**C74. Final Amen.** Paul’s affirmation + call for church’s confirmation; conflicts within and persecution without “cannot diminish the experience of God’s grace.” Letter of joy ends with blessing of grace.  
- *Locus:* slice ~295.  
- **Textual note:** Hansen prints Amen with the closing; discusses Amen as affirmation/response (also at 4:20). Slice does not develop a separate text-critical apparatus on whether Amen is original to 4:23.

---

## Absences / not claimed in this slice

- Hansen does **not** adjudicate the true companion’s identity (survey only).  
- Does **not** affirm Euodia/Syntyche as theological parties (legalist vs antinomian) or as split over Paul-support.  
- Does **not** read 4:13 as prosperity/omnipotence slogan — explicitly opposes that use.  
- Does **not** reduce Caesar’s household to imperial blood relatives.  
- Does **not** teach health-and-wealth return on giving (explicit denial).  
- Does **not** equate Christian contentment with Stoic emotional detachment/self-sufficiency without Christ.  
- No full treatment of later reception history of Euodia/Syntyche or 4:13 proof-texting beyond Hansen’s contextual correction.  
- No separate critical apparatus on 4:23 Amen beyond liturgical/affirmative function of Amen in the body text.
